**a) I/O processor (5 marks)** — a small dedicated processor that executes its own **channel program** to move data between memory and devices. The CPU writes the command list and signals the IOP, which runs independently and interrupts when finished.

```text
CPU --(channel program address)--> IOP --> memory <--> device
IOP --(interrupt on completion)--> CPU
```

It removes the per-word CPU involvement of programmed or interrupt-driven I/O, so a slow device can transfer a megabyte while the CPU keeps computing.

**b) Vector processing (5 marks)** — one instruction applies to a whole array: `C(1:n) = A(1:n) + B(1:n)`. A pipelined vector unit streams element pairs, so `n` scalar instructions become one and throughput is set by pipeline depth rather than instruction issue. CRAY-1 and today's SIMD/AVX units use it for weather models and matrix algebra.

**c) Memory interleaving (5 marks)** — memory is split into `m` banks with consecutive addresses in different banks, so `m` words are fetched in parallel; with cycle time `t` they take about `t + (m-1)*t/m` instead of `m*t`.

```text
low-order  : 0->bank 0, 1->bank 1, 2->bank 2   (maximum parallelism)
high-order : each bank holds a contiguous block     (simple, fewer conflicts)
```

It raises effective bandwidth, attacking the CPU-memory speed gap from the memory side.

**d) Loop buffer (5 marks)** — a small fast store (64-256 bytes) holding the body of the current loop. The first pass copies instructions in; later passes fetch from the buffer, saving memory bandwidth and avoiding a pipeline restart at the backward branch. Common on DSPs and low-power cores.

**a) Cache mapping techniques (6 marks)**

Mapping decides which line a memory block may occupy; the three schemes trade hardware against conflict misses.

**1. Direct mapping** — block `j` goes to line `j mod C`, so the line is fixed by the address:

```text
| tag | line number | block offset |
```

One comparator, cheap and fast, but blocks `j` and `j + C` fight for the same line — a **conflict miss** even when other lines are free.

**2. Fully associative** — a block may sit in **any** line, so the full tag is compared against every line in parallel. No conflict misses, but `C` comparators make it practical only for small caches such as a TLB.

**3. Set-associative** — `S` sets of `E` lines each; a block maps to one set and may use **any way** in it:

```text
| tag | set number | block offset |
```

| Scheme | Placement | Comparators | Conflict miss |
|---|---|---|---|
| Direct | exactly 1 line | 1 | frequent |
| Set-associative | `E` ways in a set | `E` | reduced (mainstream, 4-16 way) |
| Fully associative | any line | `C` | none |

**b) Virtual memory versus cache (4 marks)**

| Point | Cache | Virtual memory |
|---|---|---|
| Hides | CPU/main-memory speed gap | Memory/disk size gap |
| Managed by | Hardware | Operating system + MMU |
| Unit moved | Block, 32-128 B | Page, 4-8 KB |
| Miss | Refill from main memory, tens of cycles | **Page fault**, disk I/O, millions of cycles |
| Write policy | Write-through or write-back | Write-back with a dirty bit |

Both exploit **locality of reference** and move a whole block on a miss, which is why tag comparison, replacement policy and write-back appear at both levels.

**Mark distribution — Total 10 marks: a) 2 + b) 8.**

**a) Definition (2 marks)** — a **pipeline hazard** is any condition that stops the next instruction from issuing in its scheduled cycle, forcing a **stall** (bubble), so the ideal one-instruction-per-cycle throughput is lost.

**b) Types and solutions (8 marks)**

**1. Structural hazards** — two instructions need the same unit in one cycle, e.g. fetch and a data load both wanting memory, or one un-pipelined ALU.

```text
cycle 1: IF I1      cycle 2: MEM I1 and IF I2   <- memory wanted twice
```

*Fix:* separate instruction/data memories or split L1 caches, duplicate functional units, or delay the lower-priority instruction.

**2. Data hazards** — an instruction needs an operand still being produced:

```text
RAW: ADD R1,R2,R3 ; SUB R4,R1,R5   <- true dependence, the common case
WAR: SUB R4,R1,R5 ; ADD R1,R2,R3   <- must not overwrite R1 too early
WAW: ADD R1,R2,R3 ; SUB R1,R4,R5   <- final R1 must come from the later write
```

*Fix:* **forwarding (bypassing)** sends the ALU result straight to the next instruction's input, removing most RAW stalls; one **stall cycle** remains for the load-use case; the compiler reorders independent instructions into the gap; register renaming removes WAR and WAW.

**3. Control hazards** — a branch makes the next fetch address unknown until it resolves, so already-fetched instructions may be wrong:

```text
BEQ R1,R2,LABEL   ; if taken, the next 1-2 fetched instructions are discarded
```

*Fix:* **branch prediction** (static backward-taken, dynamic 2-bit counters, branch target buffer), **delayed branching** with a useful instruction in the delay slot, resolving the branch early in the ID stage, or speculative execution with rollback. A misprediction costs about the pipeline depth.
front: What do you mean by pipeline hazards/conflicts? Discuss the different types of hazards being observed and also explain the possible solutions.

**a) Characteristics of RISC architecture (5 marks)**

| Feature | RISC | CISC contrast |
|---|---|---|
| Instruction set | Small, simple (~100) | Large (~300+) |
| Instruction length | **Fixed**, e.g. 32 bits | Variable, 1-15 bytes |
| Operands | Load/store - register-to-register | Memory operands allowed |
| Registers | Many (32+) | Few, specialised |
| Cycles per instruction | ~1, pipelinable | Many, microcoded |
| Control unit | **Hardwired** | Often microprogrammed |
| Compiler role | Heavy - scheduling, allocation | Lighter |

```text
LOAD R1,(R2) ; ADD R3,R1,R4 ; STORE R3,(R5)   <- ALU touches registers only
```

A uniform format decodes in one stage, which is what makes deep pipelining and a short cycle possible.

**b(i)) Speedup ratio (2 marks)** — the non-pipelined time divided by the pipelined time:

```text
S = T(non-pipelined)/T(pipelined) = n*k/(k + (n-1))    k stages, n instructions
S -> k as n grows
```

**b(ii)) Why `S = k` is unattainable (3 marks)**

1. **Hazards** force stalls, so cycles per instruction exceed 1.
2. **Unequal stage delays** — the clock matches the *slowest* stage, so a 20 ns stage beside a 5 ns one wastes 15 ns every cycle.
3. **Fill and drain** — the first `k - 1` cycles produce nothing, which hurts short runs.
4. **Latch setup/hold and clock skew** lengthen the effective cycle.

A real 5-stage pipeline therefore delivers 3-4, not 5.

**a) Programmed I/O versus interrupt-driven I/O (4 marks)**

| Point | Programmed I/O | Interrupt-driven |
|---|---|---|
| Who waits | **CPU polls** the status flag in a loop | CPU does other work |
| Completion | Detected by reading the flag | Device raises an **interrupt** |
| CPU use | Poor - busy-waiting | Good |
| Latency | Low, deterministic | Higher, bounded by interrupt response |
| Cost | No extra hardware | Controller, vector table, context save |

```text
programmed: loop { read status; if ready then transfer }   <- CPU blocked
interrupt : start device; ...compute...; ISR transfers     <- CPU free
```

Even with interrupts each **word** costs one interrupt, which is why bulk transfers use DMA.

**b) DMA mode of data transfer (6 marks)**

A **DMA controller** moves blocks between memory and a device without the CPU handling each word. The CPU programs source, destination, count and direction once, then continues.

```text
        +------------- CPU -------------+
        |                               |  HLDA / HRQ / IRQ
   +----v-------------------------------v----+
   |            system bus                   |
   +----+--------------------------+---------+
        |                          |
   +----v-----+              +-----v------+
   |  Memory  |<------------>|    DMA     |<----> Device
   +----------+              | controller |
                             +------------+
```

1. CPU writes start address, count and direction, then issues *start*.
2. Controller asserts **HRQ**; the CPU finishes its bus cycle and answers **HLDA**, floating the bus.
3. The controller drives address and control lines, moving one word per **cycle steal** (or the whole block in **burst mode**), incrementing the address and decrementing the count.
4. At zero it releases the bus and raises an **interrupt**; the CPU reads the status.

```text
cycle stealing: one bus cycle at a time, CPU slowed slightly
burst mode    : whole block, full speed, CPU blocked
```

DMA is the only way to sustain disk and network bandwidth, at the cost of bus contention and cache-coherence care.

**i) Register addressing (2 marks)** — the operand is **in a register** named by the instruction, so no memory access occurs.

```text
ADD R1, R2, R3     ; R1 <- R2 + R3
```

The fastest mode, which is why load/store machines do almost all work in it.

**ii) Indirect addressing (2 marks)** — the instruction names a register that **holds the address** of the operand, adding one level of indirection.

```text
MOV R1, (R2)       ; R2 = 2000H, memory[2000H] = 45H  ->  R1 = 45H
```

Used for pointers and linked structures; costs an extra memory access.

**iii) Indexed addressing (2 marks)** — effective address is an **index register plus a displacement**, the natural mode for arrays.

```text
EA = IX + displacement
MOV AL, [SI + 4]   ; element 4 of the array based at SI
```

Incrementing the index walks the array without rewriting the instruction.

**iv) Base addressing (2 marks)** — effective address is a **base register plus a displacement**, used for fields of a record or locals in a stack frame.

```text
EA = BX + 8        ; 8th byte of the record based at BX
MOV AX, [BP + 4]   ; first parameter of the current function
```

Relocating a record changes only the base register.

**v) Immediate addressing (2 marks)** — the operand is a **constant inside the instruction**, so it arrives with the opcode and no operand fetch happens.

```text
MOV R1, #25        ; R1 <- 25
```

The fastest way to load a constant, but limited to the bits left in the instruction word.

**a) Booth's multiplication algorithm (6 marks)**

**Booth's algorithm** multiplies signed two's-complement numbers directly, without magnitude conversion. Adjacent multiplier bits `Q0 Q-1` select one add/subtract step, so it encodes the multiplier into signed digits.

| `Q0` | `Q-1` | Operation | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | 0 | none | inside a run of 0s |
| 0 | 1 | `A = A + M` | **end** of a run of 1s |
| 1 | 0 | `A = A - M` | **start** of a run of 1s |
| 1 | 1 | none | inside a run of 1s |

```text
        +--------------------------------+
        |  M        -M                   |
   +----v---------v------------------+    |
   |      ADD / SUBTRACT            |<---  control: Q0, Q-1
   +----+---------------------+-----+
        |                     |
   +----v-----+         +-----v----+  Q-1
   |    A     |         |    Q     |
   |  (n bit) |         |  (n bit) |
   +----+-----+         +-----+----+
        +--- arithmetic shift right A:Q:Q-1 ---+
```

```text
Algorithm Booth(M, Q, n):
  A = 0 ; Q-1 = 0 ; repeat n times:
      if Q0,Q-1 = 0,1 then A = A + M
      else if Q0,Q-1 = 1,0 then A = A - M
      arithmetic shift right A : Q : Q-1
  product = A : Q          (2n bits)
```

Each step is at most one add and one shift, and the number of adds equals the number of **runs of 1s** in the multiplier, so `0000` or `1111` needs none.

**b) `7 x (-5)` step by step (4 marks)**

`M = 00111`, `-M = 11001`, `Q = -5 = 11011`, `A = 00000`, `Q-1 = 0`.

| Step | `Q0 Q-1` | Operation | A after shift | Q after shift | `Q-1` |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| initial | - | - | `00000` | `11011` | 0 |
| 1 | 10 | `A - M` | `11100` | `11101` | 1 |
| 2 | 11 | none | `11110` | `01110` | 1 |
| 3 | 01 | `A + M` | `00010` | `10111` | 0 |
| 4 | 10 | `A - M` | `11101` | `11011` | 1 |
| 5 | 11 | none | `11110` | `11101` | 1 |

```text
A:Q = 11110 11101  ->  10-bit two's complement = -35
check: 7 x -5 = -35
```

**a) Hardwired versus microprogrammed control (5 marks)**

Both generate the same control signals; they differ in **how the pattern is stored**.

| Point | Hardwired | Microprogrammed |
|---|---|---|
| Implementation | Gates, flip-flops, counters, decoder | **Control store** of microinstructions |
| Speed | **Fast** - signals straight from gates | Slower - one ROM read per microinstruction |
| Flexibility | Fixed; a change means rewiring | **Easy** - rewrite the microcode |
| Cost | Rises steeply with instruction complexity | Cheap for complex instruction sets |
| Suited to | RISC | CISC (8086, VAX) |

```text
hardwired : IR -> decoder -> control logic -> signals
microprog : IR -> mapping -> micro-PC -> control store -> control word
```

**b) Horizontal versus vertical microprogramming (5 marks)**

The distinction is the **width and encoding** of the control word.

| Point | Horizontal | Vertical |
|---|---|---|
| Control word | **Wide**, one bit per signal | **Narrow**, signals encoded in fields |
| Bits per microinstruction | 40-100+ | 10-20 |
| Parallelism | High - many signals at once | Low |
| Decoding | None - bits drive lines directly | A decoder per field |
| Microprogram | **Short** | **Long** |
| Speed | Fast | Slower (decode delay) |

```text
horizontal: |PCout|MARin|Read|Write|...|   each bit is one control line
vertical  : | ALUop (4) | src (3) | dst (3) | next (6) |
```

**Diagonal** microprogramming is the compromise: mutually exclusive signals are encoded into fields while frequently co-asserted ones keep their own bit, balancing control-store width against decode delay.

**Components of a Computer System**

A computer system consists of hardware and software working together. The major hardware components are:

1. **Input Unit** — devices (keyboard, mouse, scanner) that accept data and instructions from the user and convert them into machine-readable form.
2. **Central Processing Unit (CPU)** — the "brain" of the computer; executes instructions and performs calculations. It contains:
   - **ALU (Arithmetic Logic Unit)** — performs arithmetic and logical operations.
   - **Control Unit (CU)** — directs the flow of data and coordinates other units.
   - **Registers** — small, fast temporary storage locations inside the CPU.
3. **Memory Unit (Primary Storage)** — RAM and ROM that store programs and data currently in use.
4. **Output Unit** — devices (monitor, printer) that present results to the user.
5. **Secondary Storage** — hard disk, SSD, optical disk for permanent storage.
6. **Buses** — pathways (address, data, control buses) that connect components and transfer data.

Software (system software like OS, and application software) runs on top of this hardware.

**Micro-operation**

A **micro-operation** is an elementary operation performed on the data stored in registers during one clock cycle. It is the basic building block of CPU operations. Examples:
- Register transfer: `R1 ← R2` (copy content of R2 into R1)
- Arithmetic: `R1 ← R1 + R2`
- Logic: `R1 ← R1 AND R2`
- Shift: `R1 ← shl R1` (shift left)

A machine instruction is implemented as a sequence of micro-operations. The control unit generates control signals to execute these micro-operations.
front: Explain the components of the Computer system and what is micro operation?

**a) Represent (12.625)₁₀ in 32-bit floating point (IEEE 754 single precision)**

Step 1 — Convert to binary:
- Integer part: 12 = `1100`
- Fraction part: 0.625 → 0.625×2 = 1.25 (1), 0.25×2 = 0.5 (0), 0.5×2 = 1.0 (1) → `.101`
- So, 12.625 = `1100.101`

Step 2 — Normalize:
`1100.101 = 1.100101 × 2³`

Step 3 — Determine fields (1 sign + 8 exponent + 23 mantissa = 32 bits):
- **Sign bit**: 0 (number is positive)
- **Exponent**: actual = 3; biased = 3 + 127 = 130 = `10000010`
- **Mantissa (fraction after the leading 1)**: `100101` padded to 23 bits = `10010100000000000000000`

**32-bit IEEE 754 representation:**
```
0 | 10000010 | 10010100000000000000000
Sign Exponent       Mantissa
```

**b) Odd parity checker**

A **parity checker** is used for error detection in data transmission/storage. An **odd parity checker** checks whether the number of 1s in the received data (including the parity bit) is odd.

- If total number of 1s is **odd** → data assumed correct (parity = 1 / no error indicated).
- If total number of 1s is **even** → an error is detected (parity = 0 / error).

For odd parity, the sender sets the parity bit so that the total count of 1s is odd. The receiver counts 1s; if the count is even, it knows at least one bit got corrupted. It can detect single-bit errors but cannot correct them or detect two-bit errors reliably.

**a) Von-Neumann Architecture**

The **Von-Neumann architecture** (stored-program concept) is the foundation of most modern computers. Proposed by John Von-Neumann, it has the following components:

```
        +---------------------+
        |      Memory         |  <-- stores both instructions and data
        | (instructions + data)|
        +----------+----------+
                   |
        +----------v----------+
        |        CPU          |
        |  +---------+-----+  |
        |  |  ALU    | CU  |  |  <-- ALU computes; Control Unit directs
        |  +---------+-----+  |
        |    +-----------+    |
        |    | Registers |    |
        |    +-----+-----+    |
        +----------+----------+
                   |
     +-------------v-------------+
     |          I/O              |
     +---------------------------+
```

**Key features:**
1. **Stored-program concept**: both program instructions and data reside in the same memory.
2. **Single memory bus**: instructions and data are fetched over the same pathway (leads to the "Von-Neumann bottleneck").
3. **Sequential execution**: instructions are fetched and executed one after another (controlled by the Program Counter).
4. **CPU components**: ALU, Control Unit, registers.
5. **Input/Output** for interaction with the user.

**b) Bus Structure with examples**

A **bus** is a shared communication pathway that transfers data, addresses and control signals between components (CPU, memory, I/O devices).

**Three types of buses:**
1. **Address Bus** — carries the address of the memory location or I/O device (unidirectional, from CPU). Example: CPU places address `2050H` on the address bus to read from that location.
2. **Data Bus** — carries actual data to be read or written (bidirectional). Example: CPU reads the byte `4AH` from memory onto the data bus.
3. **Control Bus** — carries control signals (read/write, interrupt, clock, reset). Example: `Memory Read` signal tells memory the CPU wants to read data.

**Example operation (fetching data from address 2050H):**
1. CPU puts `2050H` on the **address bus**.
2. CPU activates the **Memory Read** signal on the **control bus**.
3. Memory places the data at `2050H` onto the **data bus**.
4. CPU reads the data bus into a register.

**Flag Register of the 8086 Microprocessor**

The 8086 has a 16-bit **FLAGS register** (also called the Program Status Word). It reflects the result of arithmetic/logic operations and controls certain processor operations. It is divided into:

**1. Condition/Status flags** (set or reset by the result of operations):
| Flag | Abbreviation | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| Carry Flag | CF | Set if an arithmetic carry/borrow occurs out of the MSB |
| Parity Flag | PF | Set if the lower byte of the result has an even number of 1s |
| Auxiliary Carry Flag | AF | Set if carry/borrow occurs between bit 3 and bit 4 (BCD arithmetic) |
| Zero Flag | ZF | Set if the result of an operation is zero |
| Sign Flag | SF | Set if the MSB of the result is 1 (negative number) |

| Interrupt Enable Flag | IF | Set = maskable interrupts are enabled |
| Direction Flag | DF | Set = string operations auto-decrement; reset = auto-increment |

**Fixed-point multiplication of 23 and 17**

Using the shift-and-add (paper-and-pencil) binary multiplication algorithm:

```
        1 0 1 1 1     (23 = 10111₂)
      × 1 0 0 0 1     (17 = 10001₂)
      ---------
        1 0 1 1 1     (23 × 1)
      0 0 0 0 0       (23 × 0, shifted left 1)
    0 0 0 0 0         (23 × 0, shifted left 2)
  0 0 0 0 0           (23 × 0, shifted left 3)
1 0 1 1 1             (23 × 1, shifted left 4)
-----------------
1 1 0 0 0 0 1 1 1     = 391₁₀
```

**Result: 23 × 17 = 391** (`110000111₂`).

**Step-by-step (shift-and-add):**
1. Examine the bits of the multiplier (17 = 10001) from right to left.
2. For each 1 bit, add a shifted copy of the multiplicand (23) to the partial product.
   - Bit 0 = 1: add `23 × 2⁰` = 23
   - Bit 4 = 1: add `23 × 2⁴` = 23 × 16 = 368
3. Sum: 23 + 368 = **391**.

The fixed-point multiplication assumes fixed positions for the binary point; for integers the point is at the right, so the result is a straightforward integer product.

**a) Key characteristics of micro-programmed control**

In micro-programmed control, the control signals for each instruction are generated by a **micro-program** stored in a **control store** (a special memory).

Key characteristics:
1. **Control store**: a ROM stores micro-programs (sequences of micro-instructions) for every machine instruction.
2. **Micro-instruction**: each word contains control signals to activate specific hardware (registers, ALU function, memory read/write) plus the address of the next micro-instruction.
3. **Sequencing**: a micro-program sequencer determines the next micro-address; supports conditional branching based on flags.
4. **Easy to modify/debug**: adding a new instruction or fixing a bug means changing the micro-program, not rewiring hardware (unlike hardwired control).
5. **Slower than hardwired**: each instruction takes several clock cycles (one per micro-instruction) due to the fetch-decode-execute of micro-instructions.
6. **Uniform structure**: complex instructions are built from simple, uniform micro-steps.

**b) Types of micro-operation**

A micro-operation is an elementary operation on register contents performed in one clock cycle. Types:

| Type | Description | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Register transfer | Move data from one register to another | `R1 ← R2` |
| Arithmetic | Perform arithmetic on register data | `R1 ← R1 + R2` |
| Logic | Perform bitwise logical operation | `R1 ← R1 AND R2` |
| Shift | Shift bits in a register | `R1 ← shl R1` (shift left) |
| Memory | Read/write memory via registers | `R1 ← M[AR]` (read memory) |

Example: the instruction `ADD R1, R2` may be implemented by micro-operations:
1. `AR ← PC` (fetch address)
2. `DR ← M[AR]` (fetch instruction)
3. `R1 ← R1 + R2` (execute add)

**Cache memory mapping techniques**

Cache is a small, fast memory between the CPU and main memory. When the CPU needs data, it looks in cache first. **Mapping** decides how a block of main memory is placed into cache lines.

There are three main mapping techniques:

**1. Direct Mapping**
- Each block of main memory maps to **exactly one specific cache line** (using `block address mod number of cache lines`).
- Simple and fast; hardware cost is low.
- Disadvantage: if two frequently used blocks map to the same line, they keep replacing each other (conflict misses).
- Example: main memory block 10 → cache line `10 mod 8 = 2`.

**2. Fully Associative Mapping**
- A block of main memory can be placed in **any cache line**.
- Most flexible; no conflict misses.
- Disadvantage: expensive hardware — requires associative search of all tags in parallel; slower lookup.
- Replacement policy (e.g. LRU) needed when cache is full.

**3. Set-Associative Mapping**
- A compromise: cache is divided into **sets**, each containing a few lines (e.g. 2-way, 4-way).
- A block maps to a specific set (`block address mod number of sets`) but can go to any line within that set.
- Example: 2-way set associative — block 10 → set `10 mod S`, then placed in either line of that set.
- Reduces conflict misses compared to direct mapping, cheaper than fully associative.

Summary: Direct (fast, cheap, more conflicts) < Set-associative (balanced) < Fully associative (flexible, expensive, complex).
front: Discuss the various mapping techniques used in cache memory.

**a) What is virtual memory?**

**Virtual memory** is a memory-management technique that gives each program the illusion of having a large, contiguous private address space (virtual address space), even though the actual physical RAM may be smaller. It allows programs larger than physical memory to run by keeping only needed parts in RAM and the rest on disk.

**b) How virtual memory works**

1. **Virtual address → Physical address translation**: Every program uses virtual addresses. The **Memory Management Unit (MMU)**, with help from the OS, translates virtual addresses to physical RAM addresses at run time.
2. **Paging**: Virtual memory is divided into fixed-size **pages**; physical memory into equal-sized **frames**. A page table records which frame holds each page.
3. **Page table & TLB**: The OS maintains a page table per process. A fast hardware cache called the **TLB** (Translation Lookaside Buffer) stores recent virtual-to-physical translations to speed up access.
4. **Demand paging / swapping**: When a program references a page not in RAM (**page fault**), the OS loads that page from disk into a free frame, updates the page table, and restarts the instruction. If RAM is full, an unused page is written back to disk (**page replacement**, e.g. LRU).
5. **Benefits**: programs can exceed RAM size, multiple programs share memory safely (isolated address spaces), and memory is used efficiently.

Example: a program references virtual page 5. The MMU checks the page table → page 5 maps to frame 12 → physical address = frame 12 + offset. If page 5 is not in RAM, a page fault occurs and the OS brings it in from disk.

**a) Interfacing RAM and ROM EPROM to the 8086 microprocessor**

The 8086 has a 20-bit address bus (1 MB address space, 00000H–FFFFFH) and a 16-bit data bus. Memory chips (RAM and EPROM) are interfaced by connecting their data lines to the 8086 data bus and using an **address decoder** to generate individual chip-select (CS) signals.

Steps:
1. **Address lines** (A0–A19) from the 8086 connect to the address inputs of memory chips and to the decoder.
2. **Address decoder** (e.g., a 3-to-8 decoder) decodes the high-order address lines to produce separate CS signals for RAM and EPROM, assigning them distinct address ranges.
   - Example: EPROM mapped to the top of memory (F0000H–FFFFFH, where the 8086 starts after reset); RAM mapped to the lower region.
3. **Data lines** (D0–D15) connect the 8086 data bus to the data pins of RAM and EPROM through bus transceivers (8086/8286/8289) for driving.
4. **Control signals** (`RD`, `WR`, `M/IO`, `BHE`, `ALE`) from the 8086 and the 8288 bus controller connect to memory's output-enable and write-enable pins to control read/write cycles.
5. When the CPU places an address, the decoder activates the CS of the target chip; RD/WR then reads from or writes to that memory.

**b) Use of EPROM**

**EPROM (Erasable Programmable Read-Only Memory)** is non-volatile memory that retains data without power and can be erased by exposing it to ultraviolet (UV) light through its quartz window, then reprogrammed.

Uses:
- Stores the **BIOS / firmware** and **bootstrap program** that run when the computer starts (these rarely change).
- Stores permanent system software and lookup tables in embedded systems.
- Because it is non-volatile, the program is available immediately on power-up.

Note: EPROM erases the entire chip at once (UV), unlike EEPROM/flash which allow byte/block-level electrical erasure.

**a) Restoring division (4 marks)**

The dividend is extended to double length and shifted left into an accumulator `A`: `A` holds the partial remainder, `Q` the quotient being built.

```text
repeat n times:
    shift left A:Q
    A = A - M
    if A < 0:  restore A = A + M   and set q0 = 0
    else:                          set q0 = 1
quotient in Q, remainder in A
```

It is called *restoring* because a failed subtraction is undone. Example, `13 / 4` in 5 bits (`M = 00100`):

| i | A after op | Q | Decision |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | `00000` | `11010` | A<0, restore, q0=0 |
| 2 | `00001` | `10100` | A<0, restore, q0=0 |
| 3 | `00011` | `01000` | A<0, restore, q0=0 |
| 4 | `00010` | `10001` | q0=1 |
| 5 | `00001` | `00011` | q0=1 |

**Quotient `00011` = 3, remainder `00001` = 1.** Each step costs one add/subtract and one shift, so it runs in `O(n)` for an `n`-bit word.

**b) BIU and EU of the 8086 (4 marks)**

The 8086 splits into two pipelined halves that work in parallel:

| Unit | Role |
|---|---|
| **BIU** (Bus Interface Unit) | Fetches instructions, holds the **6-byte instruction queue**, computes 20-bit physical addresses from segment:offset, and performs all bus reads/writes |
| **EU** (Execution Unit) | Decodes and executes instructions, does ALU work, and computes effective addresses; it never touches the bus |

```text
memory --(BIU fetch)--> 6-byte queue --(EU decode/execute)--> registers
```

The split is a two-stage pipeline: while the EU executes one instruction the BIU is already fetching the next, so instruction fetch overlaps execution. A **queue flush** is needed whenever a jump or call changes the flow.

**a) Hit and miss ratio (3 marks)**

```text
hit ratio  h = (number of cache hits) / (total accesses)
miss ratio   = 1 - h
```

```text
     = 14.5 ns
```

If the cache and memory are accessed **in parallel** (exclusive convention) the formula is `h*Tc + (1-h)*Tm = 7.2 + 6.5 = 13.7 ns`.

**a) Cache memory mapping (3 marks)**

**Mapping** is the rule that decides which cache line a given main-memory block may occupy. Since the cache is far smaller than memory, many blocks compete for lines; the mapping fixes how many choices each block has, and hence both the hardware needed to search and the conflict misses that result. The three schemes are **direct**, **fully associative** and **set-associative**.

**b) Direct mapping and its disadvantage (5 marks)**

Each block maps to exactly one line, decided by the block address:

```text
| tag | line number | block offset |
line = (block address) mod (number of lines)
```

Only one tag comparator is needed, so the lookup is cheap and fast, and no replacement policy is required — there is only one candidate line.

**Main disadvantage: conflict misses.** Blocks that differ by a multiple of the number of lines map to the same line, so they evict each other alternately even though the rest of the cache is empty:

```text
cache = 4 lines;  blocks 0 and 4 both map to line 0
access 0, 4, 0, 4, 0, 4 ...  ->  every access misses
```

That thrashing can drive the miss ratio close to 100% for a strided access pattern, which is why real caches are usually 4-16 way **set-associative**: a block then has `E` candidates, which removes most conflicts at the cost of `E` comparators.

**i) TLB (4 marks)**

A **Translation Lookaside Buffer** is a small, fully associative cache of recent **page-table entries** inside the MMU. A virtual address is split into a virtual page number and an offset; the TLB is searched with the VPN, and on a hit it returns the physical frame number in one cycle instead of walking the page table in memory.

```text
virtual address -> [ TLB lookup ] --hit--> frame number  (1-2 cycles)
                             `--miss--> page-table walk (memory), then refill TLB
```

It holds 64-1024 entries, fully associative or high-way; without it every memory access would need an extra memory access for translation.

**ii) DMA (4 marks)**

**Direct Memory Access** lets a controller move a block between memory and a device without the CPU handling each word. The CPU programs address, count and direction, the controller requests the bus (**HRQ/HLDA**), transfers by cycle stealing or burst, then interrupts on completion. It is essential for disks and network cards; the cost is bus contention and cache-coherence care.

**iii) Virtual memory (4 marks)**

**Virtual memory** gives each process a large, contiguous address space that is mapped onto physical frames and backed by disk. Only resident pages stay in memory; a reference to an absent page traps to a **page fault**, and the OS loads it, evicting a victim by LRU or clock. It provides three things at once: programs larger than physical memory, **isolation** between processes, and simple relocation. The cost is the TLB lookup on every access and the huge latency of a page fault.

**a) Micro-operation (3 marks)**

A **micro-operation** is the smallest atomic step a CPU can perform in one clock: a register transfer such as `R1 <- R2`, an ALU action such as `R1 <- R1 + R2`, or a memory access such as `MAR <- PC`. Every machine instruction is decomposed into a sequence of these, and the control unit's only job is to emit the signals that realise them.

```text
instruction: ADD R1, (R2)
micro-ops:  MAR <- R2 ;  MBR <- M[MAR] ;  R1 <- R1 + MBR
```

**b) Microprogrammed control unit (5 marks)**

A **microprogrammed control unit** stores each instruction's micro-operation sequence as a **microprogram** in a control store, and executes it step by step.

```text
+-------------+     +-----------+     +----------------+     +--------------+
| instruction |---->|  mapping  |---->|  micro-PC      |---->| control store|
|  register   |     |   logic   |     | (sequencer)    |     |  (ROM)       |
+-------------+     +-----------+     +-------+--------+     +------+-------+
                                              ^                     |
                                              |   next-address field|
                                              +---------------------+
                                                                     |
                                              control signals ------> control lines
```

**Working:** the opcode in the IR enters the **mapping logic**, which produces the start address of that instruction's microprogram; the **micro-PC** fetches that microinstruction from the control store; its bits are split into the control signals (which drive the datapath) and a **next-address field** (which selects the following microinstruction, or branches on a condition flag). The sequence ends with a microinstruction that returns control to the fetch routine. Because the sequence lives in ROM, adding an instruction means adding microcode rather than rewiring — the reason CISC designs use this scheme.

**a) Restoring division algorithm (4 marks)**

For unsigned integers the dividend is held double length in `A:Q` and `M` is the divisor.

```text
repeat n times:
    shift left A:Q
    A = A - M
    if A < 0:  A = A + M (restore) ; q0 = 0
    else:                          ; q0 = 1
quotient in Q, remainder in A
```

The failed subtraction is undone — hence *restoring*. With `13 / 4` in 5 bits (`M = 00100`) the five steps give quotient `00011` = 3 and remainder `00001` = 1. Each step is one add/subtract and one shift, so the cost is `O(n)` for an `n`-bit word; the *non-restoring* variant keeps the negative remainder and corrects at the end, saving that addition.

**b) `(-9) x (-13)` using Booth's algorithm (4 marks)**

`M = -9 = 10111`, `-M = 01001`, `Q = -13 = 10011`, `A = 00000`, `Q-1 = 0` (5-bit).

| Step | `Q0 Q-1` | Operation | A after shift | Q after shift | `Q-1` |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| initial | - | - | `00000` | `10011` | 0 |
| 1 | 10 | `A - M` | `00100` | `11001` | 1 |
| 2 | 11 | none | `00010` | `01100` | 1 |
| 3 | 01 | `A + M` | `11100` | `10110` | 0 |
| 4 | 00 | none | `11110` | `01011` | 0 |
| 5 | 10 | `A - M` | `00011` | `10101` | 1 |

```text
A:Q = 00011 10101  ->  10-bit two's complement = +117
check: (-9) x (-13) = +117
```

Both operands are negative, so the signs cancel and the product is positive — Booth handles this without ever converting to magnitude form, which is exactly its advantage over shift-and-add.

**a) Pipelining (3 marks)**

**Pipelining** overlaps the stages of instruction execution, so several instructions are in flight at once and throughput rises to about one instruction per cycle.

```text
cycle :  1   2   3   4   5
IF    : I1  I2  I3  I4  I5
ID    :     I1  I2  I3  I4
EX    :         I1  I2  I3
WB    :             I1  I2
```

The speedup approaches the number of stages `k`, but latency per instruction stays `k` cycles — pipelining raises throughput, not the time of one instruction.

**b) Hazards in pipelining (5 marks)**

**Structural hazards** — two instructions need one resource in the same cycle, e.g. fetch and a load both wanting memory. *Fix:* split instruction and data caches, duplicate functional units, or stall one instruction.

**Data hazards** — an instruction needs an operand still being produced:

```text
RAW: ADD R1,R2,R3 ; SUB R4,R1,R5   <- true dependence
WAR: SUB R4,R1,R5 ; ADD R1,R2,R3   <- write too early
WAW: ADD R1,R2,R3 ; SUB R1,R4,R5   <- wrong final write
```

*Fix:* **forwarding** bypasses the ALU result to the next instruction, removing most RAW stalls; the load-use case still needs **one stall cycle**; the compiler schedules independent work into the gap; register renaming removes WAR and WAW.

**Control hazards** — a branch leaves the next fetch address unknown:

```text
BEQ R1,R2,L     ; taken -> the already-fetched instruction is discarded
```

*Fix:* branch prediction (static backward-taken, dynamic 2-bit counters, branch target buffer), a delayed branch slot, resolving the branch earlier, or speculative execution with rollback. Each misprediction costs roughly the pipeline depth.

**a) Vector processor and RISC pipeline (4 marks)**

**i) Vector processor**

A **vector processor** applies one instruction to an entire array: `C(1:n) = A(1:n) + B(1:n)`. A pipelined vector unit streams element pairs, so `n` scalar operations become one instruction and throughput is set by pipeline depth. It is the hardware behind CRAY-style supercomputers and today's SIMD units, and it pays off only on long arrays with the same operation repeated.

**ii) RISC pipeline**

The classic five stages are **IF** (fetch), **ID** (decode and read registers), **EX** (execute or compute an address), **MEM** (data access - load/store only) and **WB** (write back). Fixed-length instructions and register-only ALU operations keep the stages balanced, so one instruction retires per cycle once the pipeline is full, and hazards are handled by forwarding and prediction rather than microcode.

```text
IF -> ID -> EX -> MEM -> WB     one instruction retires per cycle once full
```

**b) Cache hit/miss and memory hierarchy (4 marks)**

**iii) Cache hit and cache miss**

A **hit** is a reference found in the cache, costing `Tc`; a **miss** must fetch the block from main memory, costing `Tm` plus the refill. With hit ratio `h`, average access time is `h*Tc + (1-h)*Tm`, so 95% hits with `Tc = 8 ns` and `Tm = 65 ns` gives about 10.9 ns — still nearly 6x a pure hit, which shows why the miss ratio dominates.

```text
h = hits/total ;   Tavg = h*Tc + (1-h)*Tm
```

**iv) Memory hierarchy**

The **memory hierarchy** stacks storage by speed and cost — registers, L1/L2/L3 cache, main memory, SSD/disk, tape — so that frequently used data sits in the fastest level. Each level caches the one below it and exploits **locality of reference**: temporal (reuse of the same address) and spatial (reuse of nearby addresses). It presents the illusion of memory nearly as large as disk at nearly the speed of the top level.

**a) Key concept of Von Neumann architecture (3 marks)**

The key concept is the **stored program**: both the instructions and the data they operate on live in the same memory, addressed by the same address space, and travel over the same bus. A program is therefore just data that the CPU fetches, decodes and executes in a serial **fetch-decode-execute** cycle, which makes the machine general-purpose — change the memory contents and it does a different job with no rewiring.

The single shared bus for instructions and data is also the architecture's limitation: the **von Neumann bottleneck**, because fetch and data access compete for one path.

**b) Internal connection between memory and the processor (5 marks)**

The processor and memory are joined by the **system bus**, three groups of lines:

| Bus | Direction | Carries |
|---|---|---|
| Address | CPU to memory (unidirectional) | the address of the selected word |
| Data | bidirectional | the instruction or operand |
| Control | bidirectional | `RD`, `WR`, `M/IO`, clock, ready, interrupt |

```text
        +-------------------+          +------------------+
        |      CPU          |          |     MEMORY       |
        |  MAR   MBR   PC   |          |   address decoder|
        +---+----+----+-----+          +---+---------+----+
   address  |    |    |        address bus |         |
            +----|----|------------------>|         |
                 |    |     data bus       |         |
                 +----|-----------------><--+         |
                      |     control bus              |
                      +----------------------------->+
```

A read proceeds in four steps:

1. The CPU places the address in the **MAR**, which drives the **address bus**.
2. It asserts `RD` (and `M/IO`) on the **control bus**.
3. Memory decodes the address, reads the word and puts it on the **data bus**.
4. The CPU latches it into the **MBR**, and a `READY` signal marks the end of the cycle.

A write reverses the direction: address and data are driven by the CPU and `WR` selects the write cycle. Because address and data lines are separate, the address is stable for the whole cycle, which is what lets memory decode it reliably. Everything is synchronised by the clock, and DMA can take over the bus by asserting `HOLD` and receiving `HLDA`.

**a) Definition (2 marks)**

An **addressing mode** is the rule a machine uses to compute the **effective address** of an operand from the fields of the instruction — it decides whether the operand is inside the instruction itself, in a register, or in memory at an address built from registers and a displacement.

**b) Addressing modes of the 8086 with examples (6 marks)**

| Mode | Effective address | Example | Typical use |
|---|---|---|---|
| Immediate | none - the value is in the instruction | `MOV AL, 25` | constants |
| Register | none - the value is in a register | `MOV AX, BX` | fastest operands |
| Direct | the address is in the instruction | `MOV AL, [2000H]` | global variables |
| Register indirect | address in `BX`, `BP`, `SI` or `DI` | `MOV AL, [BX]` | pointers |
| Based | base register + displacement | `MOV AX, [BX+8]` | record fields, locals |
| Indexed | index register + displacement | `MOV AL, [SI+4]` | array elements |
| Based indexed | base + index (+ displacement) | `MOV AL, [BX+SI+4]` | 2-D arrays |
| String | implied `SI`/`DI`, `DF` sets direction | `MOVSB`, `CMPSB` | block moves |

```text
EA = (BX or BP) + (SI or DI) + displacement     ;  displacement 0, 8 or 16 bit
effective segment: BX/SI/DI -> DS ,  BP/SP -> SS
MOV AL, [BX+SI+4]      EA = BX + SI + 4
```

Two restrictions shape the design: only **one** memory operand is allowed per instruction, and the base must come from `BX`/`BP` while the index comes from `SI`/`DI` — which is still enough to address a matrix element or a structure field in one instruction. The default-segment rule means a `BP`-based access automatically reaches the stack frame, so a compiler needs no segment override for locals and parameters. Immediate and register modes need no memory reference at all, which is why they are used for constants and hot variables.

**a) Pipelining (2 marks)**

**Pipelining** decomposes instruction execution into stages and overlaps them, so while one instruction executes, the next is being decoded and a third fetched. Throughput rises to about one instruction per cycle, though each instruction still takes as many cycles as there are stages.

**b) RISC versus CISC (3 marks)**

| Point | RISC | CISC |
|---|---|---|
| Instruction set | small, simple | large, complex |
| Length | fixed | variable |
| ALU operands | registers only (load/store) | memory allowed |
| Registers | many | few |
| Cycles per instruction | ~1 | many |
| Control unit | hardwired | microprogrammed |

```text
CISC: ADD [BX], AX                                   one instruction, several micro-ops
RISC: LOAD R1,(R2) ; ADD R3,R1,R4 ; STORE R3,(R2)    three instructions, clean pipeline
```

**c) Pipeline hazards (3 marks)**

| Hazard | Cause | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| Structural | two instructions need one unit | split caches, duplicate units |
| Data (RAW) | operand not yet produced | forwarding, one stall for load-use |
| Data (WAR/WAW) | out-of-order writes | register renaming |
| Control | branch target unknown | prediction, delayed branch, speculation |

```text
RAW: ADD R1,R2,R3 ; SUB R4,R1,R5    the SUB must wait for R1 or receive it by forwarding
```

A hazard forces a **stall** (bubble), so cycles per instruction exceed one; that stall rate, together with unequal stage delays, is why a k-stage pipeline achieves well below a k-fold speedup.

**a) BIU and EU of the 8086 (5 marks)**

The 8086 is internally split into two units that work concurrently:

| Unit | Functions |
|---|---|
| **BIU** (Bus Interface Unit) | holds `CS DS SS ES` and `IP`; builds the 20-bit physical address; fetches instructions into the **6-byte queue**; performs all bus reads and writes |
| **EU** (Execution Unit) | decodes instructions from the queue; runs the ALU and sets flags; computes effective addresses; holds `AX BX CX DX SP BP SI DI` |

```text
            +--------------------------------------------+
  bus <---->| BIU:  CS DS SS ES  |  IP  | 6-byte queue    |
            +----------------------+---------------------+
                                   | queue
            +----------------------v---------------------+
            | EU: AX BX CX DX  SP BP SI DI | ALU | FLAGS   |
            +--------------------------------------------+

physical address = segment register x 16 + offset
```

The BIU prefetches while the EU executes, so instruction fetch overlaps execution — effectively a two-stage pipeline, and the reason a taken branch costs time (the queue must be flushed). Because the segment registers are shifted left by 4 before the offset is added, two 16-bit registers produce a 20-bit address, giving 1 MB of addressable memory.

**b) Maximum and minimum modes (3 marks)**

| Point | Minimum mode | Maximum mode |
|---|---|---|
| `MN/MX` | tied high | tied low |
| Control signals | generated by the **8086 itself** | generated by an external **8288** |
| Status pins | `IO/M`, `WR`, `RD` used directly | `S0-S2` decoded by the 8288 |
| Systems | single processor | multiprocessor with 8087 or DMA |
| Extra signals | none | `LOCK`, `RQ/GT`, `QS0-QS1` |

```text
minimum: 8086 --(ALE,RD,WR,IO/M)--> memory and I/O
maximum: 8086 --(S0-S2)--> 8288 --> bus control ; other masters arbitrate via RQ/GT
```

Maximum mode exists precisely so that another bus master can take over — impossible when the CPU drives the control lines itself.

**a) Direct mapping technique (5 marks)**

In **direct mapping** each main-memory block has exactly one possible cache line, fixed by the block address:

```text
line = (block address) mod (number of cache lines)

| tag | line number | block offset |
```

When a block is loaded, its **tag** (the high address bits) is stored beside the line's data. A reference splits the address into the line number, which selects the line, and the tag, which is compared with the stored tag: equal means a hit, and a mismatch means the line holds a different block and must be replaced.

```text
address 12 bits: | tag (5) | line (4) | offset (3) |
   16 lines of 8 bytes = 128 bytes total cache
```

**Advantages:** one comparator only, so the lookup is the fastest and cheapest of the three schemes, and no replacement policy is needed because there is only one candidate line.

**Disadvantage:** **conflict misses.** Blocks whose addresses differ by a multiple of the number of lines map to the same line and evict each other repeatedly, even when the rest of the cache is empty — a strided access over such a distance can make the miss ratio close to 100%. That is why real caches are 4-16 way set-associative.

**b) Virtual memory (3 marks)**

**Virtual memory** gives each process a large, contiguous **virtual address space** that the MMU maps onto physical frames, with disk as backing store. Only resident pages stay in memory; a reference to an absent page traps as a **page fault**, and the OS loads it, evicting a victim by LRU or clock while the **TLB** caches recent translations.

```text
virtual address -> MMU/TLB -> physical address -> frame in memory (else page fault -> disk)
```

It provides three things at once: programs larger than physical memory, **isolation** between processes, and simple relocation — at the cost of a translation on every access.

**a) Fixed point versus floating point (4 marks)**

| Point | Fixed point | Floating point |
|---|---|---|
| Radix position | implicit and fixed | stored in the exponent |
| Format | sign + integer part (+ implied fraction) | sign + biased exponent + significand |
| Range | narrow | very wide |
| Precision | constant across the range | varies with magnitude |
| Operations | plain integer ALU | FPU: align, normalise, round |
| Speed and cost | fast, cheap, exact for money | slower, rounding error |
| Typical use | DSP, embedded, currency | scientific, graphics, ML |

```text
fixed   8.8 : 00000011.10010000            = 3.5625 exactly
float 32    : | S | E (8) | M (23) |        huge range, ~7 digits of precision
```

A fixed-point value always keeps the same number of fractional bits, so it cannot represent both `10^-6` and `10^6`; floating point shifts the radix per value, trading precision for range.

**b) IEEE 754 single and double precision (4 marks)**

```text
single (32): | S |  E (8)  |          M (23)          |
double (64): | S |  E (11) |          M (52)          |
value = (-1)^S x 1.M x 2^(E - bias)     bias = 127 (single), 1023 (double)
```

| Field | Single | Double |
|---|---|---|
| Sign | 1 bit | 1 bit |
| Biased exponent | 8 bits | 11 bits |
| Fraction | 23 bits | 52 bits |
| Precision | ~7 decimal digits | ~16 decimal digits |
| Range | 1.2e-38 to 3.4e+38 | 2.2e-308 to 1.8e+308 |

The **hidden leading 1** of a normalised number is not stored, so 23 stored bits give 24 significant bits. All-zero and all-one exponents are reserved for zero, subnormals, infinity and NaN.

```text
-6.5 -> 6.5 = 110.1b = 1.101 x 2^2 ; E = 2+127 = 129 = 10000001
single: 1 10000001 10100000000000000000000
```

**a) Arithmetic Shift Right (2 marks)**

An **arithmetic shift right** moves every bit one place right and **replicates the sign bit** into the vacated most-significant position, so a negative number stays negative.

```text
1110 1000  (-24)  >> 1   ->   1111 0100  (-12)     sign 1 copied in

0110 1000  (104)  >> 1   ->   0011 0100  ( 52)     sign 0 copied in
```

It is the standard step in restoring division and Booth multiplication, and it computes `floor(n / 2)` for two's-complement values — unlike a logical shift, which would turn a negative number into a large positive one.

**b) `(-11) x (-9)` using Booth's algorithm (6 marks)**

`M = -11 = 10101`, `-M = 01011`, `Q = -9 = 10111`, `A = 00000`, `Q-1 = 0` (5-bit operands).

| Step | `Q0 Q-1` | Operation | A after shift | Q after shift | `Q-1` |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| initial | - | - | `00000` | `10111` | 0 |
| 1 | 10 | `A - M` | `00101` | `11011` | 1 |
| 2 | 11 | none | `00010` | `11101` | 1 |
| 3 | 11 | none | `00001` | `01110` | 1 |
| 4 | 01 | `A + M` | `11011` | `00111` | 0 |
| 5 | 10 | `A - M` | `00011` | `00011` | 1 |

```text
A:Q = 00011 00011   ->   10-bit two's complement = +99
check: (-11) x (-9) = +99
```

Only three of the five steps needed an add/subtract, because the multiplier `10111` contains one run of 1s; a 5-bit multiplier of all 1s would need none. Booth therefore adapts its work to the operand pattern instead of always performing `n` additions, and it never converts to magnitude form, so it handles mixed signs uniformly.

**Mark distribution — Total 8 marks: a) 2 + b) 6.**

**a) Instruction cycle (2 marks)**

The **instruction cycle** is the loop the CPU repeats for every instruction: **fetch** the instruction at the address in the PC, **decode** the opcode, **fetch operands**, **execute**, and **store** the result while updating the PC. An interrupt between instructions diverts the loop to an interrupt service routine.

**b) Functional block diagram of the control memory (6 marks)**

```text
  +--------------+      +-------------+      +----------------------+
  |  Instruction |      |   Mapping   |      |   Control Memory     |
  |  Register    |----->|    Logic    |----->|  (control store ROM) |
  +--------------+      +-------------+      +----------+-----------+
                                 ^                      |
                                 |            +---------v-----------+
                        +--------+--------+   | Control Data Register|
                        |    Micro-PC     |<--+  (microinstruction)  |
                        |   (sequencer)   |   +----+-----------+-----+
                        +--------+--------+        |           |
                                 ^                 v           v
                        next-address field   control      next-address
                        / branch condition   signals      field
```

The five functional blocks are the **instruction register**, the **mapping logic**, the **control memory** (ROM), the **control data register** and the **micro-PC / sequencer**.

**Working:** the opcode enters the mapping logic, which yields the start address of that instruction's microprogram. The micro-PC supplies the address to the control memory, whose word is latched in the control data register. Its bits split into the **control signals** that drive the datapath (gate a register onto the bus, select the ALU operation, write memory) and the **next-address field**, which with the sequencer and any branch condition picks the next microinstruction.

```text
address -> control memory -> microinstruction -> { control signals , next address }
                                              `-> micro-PC -> next address
```

The sequence finishes with a microinstruction that returns the micro-PC to the fetch routine. Because the whole instruction set lives in this ROM, adding an instruction means adding microcode rather than rewiring — the defining advantage of microprogrammed control.

**Mark distribution — Total 8 marks: a) 4 + b) 4.**

Six notes follow, so whichever two you choose per part are complete.

**a) First pair (4 marks)**

**Flynn's classification** groups computers by how many instruction and data streams they handle at once: **SISD** (one instruction, one datum — a classic CPU), **SIMD** (one instruction over many data — vector units, GPUs), **MISD** (many instructions on one datum — rare, systolic arrays) and **MIMD** (many of both — multicore CPUs, clusters). It is coarse but captures the step from scalar to vector to parallel processing.

**RISC pipelining** overlaps five balanced stages — **IF, ID, EX, MEM, WB** — so one instruction retires per cycle once the pipeline is full. Fixed-length instructions and register-only ALU operations keep the stages equal, and hazards are handled by forwarding and branch prediction rather than microcode.

**b) Second pair (4 marks)**

**Memory hierarchy** stacks registers, L1/L2/L3 cache, main memory, SSD and disk so that hot data sits in the fastest level. Each level caches the one below and exploits **locality of reference** — temporal (same address reused) and spatial (nearby addresses reused) — presenting memory nearly as large as disk at nearly the speed of the top level.

**TLB (Translation Lookaside Buffer)** is a small fully associative cache of recent page-table entries inside the MMU. A virtual address is split into a virtual page number and an offset; a TLB hit returns the frame number in a cycle, while a miss walks the page table in memory. It is essential because without it every memory access would cost an extra memory access for translation.

**Cache hit and miss** — a hit is a reference found in cache, costing `Tc`; a miss must fetch the block from main memory at cost `Tm`. With hit ratio `h`, average access time is `h*Tc + (1-h)*Tm`, so 95% hits at `Tc = 8 ns` and `Tm = 65 ns` gives about 10.9 ns — nearly 6x a pure hit, which is why the miss ratio dominates cache design.
